questions.explanation: A seed can stay dormant for days or years until conditions favor germination. It carries a supply of stored food for the embryo. Wind or animals can carry it a long distance from the parent plant. Sperm swimming through water is how seedless plants reproduce, and seeds remove that requirement. A spore is a single cell with no stored food. A seed is a multicellular embryo with food and a protective coat.

options: The transfer of a pollen grain, the male gametophyte, to an ovule.

questions.answer: The transfer of a pollen grain, the male gametophyte, to an ovule.
questions.explanation: Pollination is the transfer of a pollen grain to an ovule. The pollen grain is the male gametophyte. Releasing spores from a sporangium is how seedless plants reproduce. In flowering plants, the pollen grain usually lands on the stigma first, and a pollen tube then grows to the ovule. prompt.text: A fern gametophyte is a small green plant living on its own. A pine's gametophytes stay inside the parent and can be seen only with a microscope. What is true of all seed plants?

options: Unlike their ancestors, seed plants have microscopic gametophytes.
Unlike their ancestors, seed plants have large free-living gametophytes.
Seed plants have no gametophyte. The sporophyte makes the gametes.
The gametophyte is the dominant body, and the sporophyte grows on it.
questions.answer: Unlike their ancestors, seed plants have microscopic gametophytes.
questions.explanation: All seed plants have reduced gametophytes. Unlike their ancestors, those gametophytes are microscopic and stay inside the parent sporophyte. A fern gametophyte is small, but it lives on its own and is not the seed-plant pattern. A dominant gametophyte with the sporophyte growing on it is the bryophyte pattern. Seed plants still have a gametophyte. The sporophyte makes spores by meiosis. The gametophyte makes the gametes.

prompt.text: Which spore condition do all seed plants share?

options: Heterospory. They produce both megaspores and microspores.
Homospory. They produce one kind of spore that develops into a bisexual gametophyte.
They produce only microspores.
They produce only megaspores.
questions.answer: Heterospory. They produce both megaspores and microspores.
questions.explanation: All seed plants are heterosporous. They produce megaspores and microspores. Homospory is one spore type that typically develops into a bisexual gametophyte, which is the pattern of many seedless plants. A plant that made only microspores, or only megaspores, would not be heterosporous. Some seedless vascular plants, such as Selaginella, are also heterosporous. Heterospory is shared by every seed plant, and it is not limited to seed plants.

prompt.text: A pine tree carries both pollen cones and seed cones. In a cycad population, some plants produce only pollen cones and others produce only seed cones. What is the distinction?

options: The pine is monoecious: male and female structures are on the same plant. The cycads are dioecious: those structures are on separate plants.
The pine is dioecious: male and female structures are on separate plants. The cycads are monoecious: both structures are on the same plant.
The pine is heterosporous. The cycads are homosporous.
The pine has a dominant sporophyte. The cycads have a dominant gametophyte.
questions.answer: The pine is monoecious: male and female structures are on the same plant. The cycads are dioecious: those structures are on separate plants.
questions.explanation: A monoecious plant has male and female reproductive structures on the same individual. A pine carries both pollen cones and seed cones, so it is monoecious. A dioecious species has those structures on separate plants. One cycad produces only pollen cones, and another produces only seed cones. Ginkgos are dioecious as well. Calling the pine dioecious and the cycads monoecious swaps the two terms. Heterospory means a plant makes both megaspores and microspores. All seed plants are heterosporous, whether they are monoecious or dioecious. A dominant sporophyte and a microscopic gametophyte is the pattern of every seed plant, including both the pine and the cycads.

prompt.text: Which description fits the reproductive cycle of a pine?

options: The pine tree is the sporophyte. Pollen cones produce pollen grains, the male gametophytes. Seed cones bear ovules, and a megaspore inside an ovule develops into the female gametophyte. More than a year after pollination, a pollen tube delivers nonmotile sperm to an egg. The fertilized ovule becomes a seed on the cone scale.
The gametophyte is the pine tree. A dependent sporophyte grows on it and releases spores from a capsule.
One kind of spore grows into a free-living bisexual gametophyte, and flagellated sperm swim to the egg through water outside the plant.
Pollination and fertilization happen together. The fertilized ovule becomes a seed enclosed in a fruit.
questions.answer: The pine tree is the sporophyte. Pollen cones produce pollen grains, the male gametophytes. Seed cones bear ovules, and a megaspore inside an ovule develops into the female gametophyte. More than a year after pollination, a pollen tube delivers nonmotile sperm to an egg. The fertilized ovule becomes a seed on the cone scale.
questions.explanation: A pine tree is the sporophyte. It is monoecious, so pollen cones and seed cones are on the same tree. Meiosis in a pollen cone produces microspores, and each microspore develops into a pollen grain, the male gametophyte. In a seed cone, a megasporocyte inside an ovule produces four megaspores and one persists. That megaspore develops into the female gametophyte, which makes eggs. Wind carries pollen to the ovule. The pollen tube grows inside the ovule and delivers nonmotile sperm. Fertilization happens more than a year after pollination. The fertilized ovule is the seed, and it sits exposed on the cone scale. A dominant gametophyte with a spore capsule is the bryophyte pattern. One spore type, a free-living bisexual gametophyte, and sperm that swim through outside water is the homosporous seedless-plant pattern. Cycads and ginkgos have flagellated sperm. A seed enclosed in a fruit, with fertilization soon after pollination, is the flowering-plant pattern.

questions.answer: Each grain has two wings, or air bladders, that carry it on the wind.
questions.explanation: A pine pollen grain has two wings, one on each side of the body. These wings are air bladders, and they carry the grain on the wind to a seed cone. The grain is the male gametophyte. It does not swim. Cycads and ginkgos have flagellated sperm. A megaspore develops into the female gametophyte. A seed is a fertilized ovule, and in a pine it sits on the cone scale.

options: It consists primarily of tracheids and lacks vessel elements.
It consists primarily of vessel elements and lacks tracheids.

questions.answer: It consists primarily of tracheids and lacks vessel elements.
questions.explanation: Soft wood consists primarily of tracheids and lacks vessel elements. Tracheids are the least derived xylem cells, and they conduct water. This is the wood of conifers and other gymnosperms. Vessel elements arose later, in flowering plants. Wood that contains vessel elements is called hardwood. Sieve-tube elements are living phloem cells that conduct sugars. They are not the cells that make wood. Water-conducting cells in wood have lignin in their walls. Cells that conduct water and lack lignin are hydroids in some mosses, and those mosses do not make wood.

prompt.text: What is the role of resin in trees?

It conducts water through the wood.
It conducts sugars from leaves to roots.
It is the stored food inside a seed.
questions.answer: It is an antiseptic and an insect deterrent.
questions.explanation: Resin is an antiseptic and an insect deterrent. In a conifer, it seals a wound and slows bacteria and fungi, and it deters insects that would bore into the tree. Water moves through tracheids in the wood. Sugars move through sieve-tube elements in the phloem. The stored food in a seed feeds the embryo. Resin does none of those jobs.

options: One sperm joins the egg and forms the zygote. The other sperm joins the two polar nuclei and forms the endosperm.

questions.answer: One sperm joins the egg and forms the zygote. The other sperm joins the two polar nuclei and forms the endosperm.
questions.explanation: Double fertilization happens in a flowering plant, inside the embryo sac. Two sperm travel in the pollen tube. One sperm joins the egg, and that fusion forms the zygote. The endosperm is triploid, because the sperm and each polar nucleus are haploid. A single fusion, one sperm with the egg and no fusion with the polar nuclei, is what happens in a pine. The integument becomes the seed coat, and the ovary wall becomes the fruit.

It forms in double fertilization, when one sperm joins the two polar nuclei, and it is the seed's supply of stored food. Gymnosperms also make seeds with stored food, but that food is tissue of the female gametophyte. A pine does not make endosperm.

Gymnosperms are woody and slow-growing. Angiosperms are herbaceous and fast-growing. A gymnosperm stem thickens by secondary growth from a vascular cambium, and almost all gymnosperms are woody. A herbaceous body and fast growth go together in angiosperms.
Angiosperms are herbaceous and fast-growing. Gymnosperms are woody and slow-growing. A herbaceous plant does not build a thick woody trunk. A woody body and slow growth go together in gymnosperms.

Gymnosperms have lengthy reproductive cycles. Angiosperms have short reproductive cycles. In a pine, fertilization happens more than a year after pollination, and the seed then forms on the cone scale. A flowering plant can be pollinated and fertilized in one season.

Angiosperms have short reproductive cycles. Gymnosperms have lengthy reproductive cycles. A flower can be pollinated and fertilized in one season, and the fertilized ovule becomes a seed inside a fruit. In a pine, fertilization happens more than a year after pollination.

Gymnosperms have a long juvenile stage. Angiosperms have a short juvenile stage. The juvenile stage is the period before the plant can reproduce. In gymnosperms it goes with slow growth and lengthy reproductive cycles. In angiosperms a short juvenile stage goes with fast growth and short reproductive cycles.

Angiosperms have a short juvenile stage. Gymnosperms have a long juvenile stage. A short juvenile stage means the plant can reproduce sooner. In angiosperms it goes with fast growth and short reproductive cycles. In gymnosperms a long juvenile stage goes with slow growth.

prompt.text: Cotyledons and young leaves are thick, green, energetically expensive to make, and not changeable in shape

questions.explanation: Gymnosperm cotyledons and young leaves are thick, green, energetically expensive to make, and not changeable in shape. Angiosperm cotyledons and leaves are thin, deciduous, energetically cheap to make, and variable in shape. A cotyledon is a seed leaf. The gymnosperm version costs more to build and keeps one shape.

questions.explanation: Angiosperm cotyledons and leaves are thin, deciduous, energetically cheap to make, and variable in shape. Gymnosperm cotyledons and young leaves are thick, green, energetically expensive to make, and not changeable in shape. Deciduous leaves are shed. A cotyledon is a seed leaf. The angiosperm version costs less to build and can take more than one shape.

questions.explanation: Gymnosperm tracheids and sieve tubes are relatively inefficient. Angiosperm vessels and sieve tubes are highly efficient. Tracheids conduct water and are the wood of a gymnosperm. Soft wood consists primarily of tracheids and lacks vessel elements. Sieve tubes conduct sugars. Vessel elements arose later, in flowering plants, and that combination is the more efficient one.

questions.explanation: Angiosperm vessels and sieve tubes are highly efficient. Gymnosperm tracheids and sieve tubes are relatively inefficient. Vessel elements conduct water and arose in flowering plants. A gymnosperm's wood consists primarily of tracheids and lacks vessel elements. Sieve tubes conduct sugars in both groups. The efficiency difference is the vessels.

Gymnosperms have a slow seedling growth rate. Angiosperms have a rapid seedling growth rate. A gymnosperm seedling also has thick, costly cotyledons and a long juvenile stage. An angiosperm seedling has thin, cheap cotyledons and a short juvenile stage, so it grows faster.

Angiosperms have a rapid seedling growth rate. Gymnosperms have a slow seedling growth rate. Thin, cheap, deciduous cotyledons and a short juvenile stage fit the faster angiosperm seedling. Thick, costly cotyledons and a long juvenile stage fit the slower gymnosperm seedling.

prompt.text: What are the components of a seed?

options: An embryo, a supply of stored food, and a seed coat.
A pollen grain, a stigma, and a style.
An ovary, a petal, and a sepal.
A megaspore, a microspore, and an integument that has not yet become a coat.
questions.answer: An embryo, a supply of stored food, and a seed coat.
questions.explanation: A seed is a fertilized ovule. It contains an embryo, a supply of stored food, and a seed coat. The seed coat develops from the integument. In a flowering plant the stored food is endosperm, or food the endosperm passed to the cotyledons. In a pine the stored food is tissue of the female gametophyte, not endosperm. A pollen grain is the male gametophyte. An ovary wall becomes a fruit in a flowering plant. A megaspore develops into the female gametophyte before fertilization.

prompt.text: In a pine seed, what is the supply of stored food?

options: Tissue of the female gametophyte.
Endosperm formed when a sperm joins two polar nuclei.
The seed coat.
The embryo itself.
questions.explanation: In a pine seed the stored food is tissue of the female gametophyte. A pine does not make endosperm. Endosperm is the stored food of a flowering plant, formed when one sperm joins the two polar nuclei. The seed coat is the protective layer from the integument. The embryo is the new sporophyte, and it uses the stored food. It is not the food supply.

prompt.text: How do the ovules differ between a pine and a flowering plant?

options: Pine ovules are exposed on a cone scale. Flowering-plant ovules are enclosed in an ovary.
Pine ovules are enclosed in an ovary that becomes a fruit. Flowering-plant ovules are exposed on a cone scale.
A pine has no ovules. Only flowering plants have ovules.
Both enclose the ovule in an ovary. Only the flowering plant makes endosperm.
questions.answer: Pine ovules are exposed on a cone scale. Flowering-plant ovules are enclosed in an ovary.
questions.explanation: A pine is a gymnosperm, so its ovules and later its seeds are exposed, often on a cone scale. They are not enclosed in an ovary, and no fruit forms. A flowering plant encloses its ovules in an ovary, and that ovary becomes the fruit. Both plants have ovules. Endosperm is a flowering-plant tissue. It is not the reason the ovules are enclosed.

prompt.text: How does pollination differ between a pine and a flower?

options: Pine pollen is delivered to the ovule. In a flower the pollen grain lands on the stigma.
Pine pollen lands on a stigma. In a flower the pollen grain is delivered straight to the ovule.
A pine is pollinated when a sperm joins an egg. A flower is pollinated when pollen lands on the stigma.
Both deliver pollen to a stigma. Only the pine then grows a pollen tube.
questions.answer: Pine pollen is delivered to the ovule. In a flower the pollen grain lands on the stigma.
questions.explanation: A pine has no stigma. Wind carries its winged pollen grain to an ovule on a cone scale, and the pollen tube grows inside that ovule. In a flower the pollen grain, the male gametophyte, lands on the stigma. A tube then grows down the style to an ovule. Joining of a sperm with an egg is fertilization, which comes after pollination. A pine does not have a stigma.

prompt.text: How does fertilization differ between a pine and a flowering plant?

options: In a pine, a pollen tube delivers nonmotile sperm to an egg more than a year after pollination. In a flowering plant, one sperm joins the egg and the other joins the two polar nuclei.
In a pine, one sperm joins the egg and the other joins two polar nuclei. In a flowering plant, a single sperm joins the egg more than a year later.
In both, flagellated sperm swim through water outside the plant to reach the egg.
In a pine, fertilization is the landing of pollen on the ovule. In a flowering plant, fertilization is the landing of pollen on the stigma.
questions.answer: In a pine, a pollen tube delivers nonmotile sperm to an egg more than a year after pollination. In a flowering plant, one sperm joins the egg and the other joins the two polar nuclei.
questions.explanation: In a pine, fertilization is one fusion: nonmotile sperm, delivered by a pollen tube, join an egg. It happens more than a year after pollination. There is no second fusion and no endosperm. In a flowering plant, fertilization is double. One sperm joins the egg and forms the zygote. The other joins the two polar nuclei and forms the endosperm. Cycads and ginkgos, which are other gymnosperms, have flagellated sperm. Those sperm swim a short distance inside the ovule. They do not swim through water outside the plant. Landing of pollen is pollination, not fertilization.

prompt.text: How does seed dispersal differ between a pine and a flowering plant?

options: A pine seed is released from a cone scale. A flowering-plant seed is enclosed in a fruit.
A pine seed is enclosed in a fruit. A flowering-plant seed is released from a cone scale.
Both enclose the seed in a fruit. Only the pine fruit is woody.
A pine disperses spores from a sporangium. A flowering plant disperses a naked seed.
questions.answer: A pine seed is released from a cone scale. A flowering-plant seed is enclosed in a fruit.
questions.explanation: A pine seed sits exposed on the cone scale, and that is how it leaves the parent. A flowering-plant seed is enclosed in a fruit, the mature ovary, and the fruit helps move the seed. A pine does not make a fruit. A flowering plant does not carry its seeds on a cone scale. Spore release is the seedless-plant pattern.

prompt.text: Which traits help explain why angiosperms became the dominant plants?

options: They often grow fast, with a short reproductive cycle, a short juvenile stage, and efficient vessels.
They are woody and slow-growing, with a long juvenile stage and tracheids rather than vessels.
Their seeds are exposed on cone scales, and fertilization takes more than a year.
Flagellated sperm swim to the egg through water outside the plant.
questions.answer: They often grow fast, with a short reproductive cycle, a short juvenile stage, and efficient vessels.
questions.explanation: Angiosperms are often herbaceous and fast-growing. They have short reproductive cycles, a short juvenile stage, thin cheap leaves, efficient vessels, and rapid seedling growth. Those traits help explain their dominance. Woody, slow growth, long cycles, a long juvenile stage, and tracheids rather than vessels are the gymnosperm pattern. Exposed seeds on cone scales and fertilization more than a year after pollination are the pine pattern. Flagellated sperm that swim through water outside the plant are the seedless-plant pattern. Cycad and ginkgo sperm swim only inside the ovule.
